name: LiveMCPBench: Can Agents Navigate an Ocean of MCP Tools?
venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2508.01780, cs.AI / cs.CL; v1 submitted 3 Aug 2025, v2 revised 26 Feb 2026; DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2508.01780). DBLP: journals/corr/abs-2508-01780. No peer-reviewed venue listed as of the latest version; the LaTeX template carries placeholder ACM conference fields ('Woodstock, NY 2018'), indicating an ACM-style submission, but no confirmed acceptance.

Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ICIP/LiveMCPBench . Docker image: https://hub.docker.com/r/hysdhlx/livemcpbench . Project page: https://icip-cas.github.io/LiveMCPBench .
maintained_repo_url: https://github.com/icip-cas/LiveMCPBench (101 stars, 16 forks at access time; last substantive commit Dec 2025 'fix(tools): remove error bing tools') plus a public Google Sheets leaderboard: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1EXpgXq1VKw5A7l7-N2E9xt3w0eLJ2YPVPT-VrRxKZBw . The leaderboard is updated with additional models (e.g. GLM-4.5, GPT-5-Mini, Kimi-K2 added 8/18/2025).
task_domain: tool-use (agentic tool retrieval and composition over a large-scale Model Context Protocol (MCP) toolset). Touches planning/decision-making: a multi-step ReAct agent must plan which tools to retrieve and how to compose them to accomplish realistic daily tasks across six domains (Office, Lifestyle, Leisure, Finance, Travel, Shopping).
problem_setting: Interactive, single-agent, multi-step tool-use evaluation in a dynamic, large-scale, real (non-simulated) MCP environment. The agent (MCP Copilot Agent) faces 95 multi-step daily tasks and must, from a pool of 70 MCP servers / 527 tools that do NOT fit in context, retrieve relevant tools and compose multiple tool calls to solve each task. The authors formulate tool retrieval+invocation as a POMDP with hidden task states, observations from retrieved tool descriptions and execution feedback, a language action space, transitions, and a task-success reward. The agent is given only a Route action (retrieve k candidate tools), an Execute action (invoke a chosen tool), and a Response action (terminate). Tasks are deliberately dynamic (depend on evolving real-time data such as weather/news/stock prices) and long-horizon (require chaining tools). Supervision: none for the models being benchmarked (zero-shot prompting of off-the-shelf frontier LLMs at temperature 0.7); human annotation supplies 95 tasks with verified key points and serves as ground truth for validating the LLM-as-a-Judge evaluator. This is primarily a BENCHMARK + a baseline agent, not a new learning method.
what_is_retrieved: tools (MCP server-tool entries): the retrievable units are MCP tools, each embedded in a server-tool hierarchy with contextual descriptions. The Route action returns the top-k candidate tools (with their server context and descriptions) from the full LiveMCPTool suite (70 servers, 527 tools); the agent then reads these tool descriptions to decide which to Execute.
retrieval_grounding: STATIC external corpus: retrieval targets a fixed, curated tool library (LiveMCPTool: 70 MCP servers, 527 tools), packaged in a frozen, validated Docker environment for reproducibility. It is NOT an agent-written growing/episodic memory; the agent does not add tools to the store at test time. (The framework is described as open/expandable for future benchmark growth, but within an evaluation run the toolset is fixed.)
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Fixed top-k ranking objective per retrieval call (k=5 candidate tools by default), but task success requires multi-tool completeness across the multi-step rollout: each Route call returns a top-k list, and the agent must, over repeated Route+Execute steps, recover and compose the complete minimal set of tools needed for a long-horizon daily task. Retrieval is the dominant failure mode (Retrieve Error = 50% of all errors), and a k-ablation shows k=1 hurts (78.95%->64.21%) while k=10 gives no gain over k=5 (78.95%, p=1.00), indicating that completeness of the candidate set, not just top-1 ranking, matters but saturates due to retriever limits rather than candidate scarcity.
cbr_cycle_coverage: [Retrieve: yes (Route retrieves top-k tools from the toolset), Reuse: partial (retrieved tool descriptions are reused to format Execute calls, but these are TOOLS, not prior solved problem-solution cases), Revise: no, Retain: no]. Not a case-based-reasoning system; it retrieves tools, not cases.
explicit_cbr_grounding: False: the paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner. It is an MCP tool-use benchmark with dense-embedding tool retrieval (hierarchical server-tool scoring from MCP-Zero).
retrieval_unit: tool-API entry within a server-tool hierarchy: the granularity is one MCP tool (its name, parameters, and description) nested under its parent MCP server. Retrieval scoring (from MCP-Zero) combines a server-level similarity and a tool-level similarity, so the effective retrievable unit is the (server, tool) pair, surfaced as a top-k tool candidate list.
index_source: Static corpus built offline then warmed up at setup: LiveMCPTool aggregates 5,588 server configurations from the mcp.so MCP Marketplace, filters out key-dependent servers, taxonomically organizes the survivors, manually vets quality, and packages 70 servers / 527 tools into a Docker environment. The retrievable index is built offline from server/tool descriptions; the agent indexes the servers in a warm-up step (repo: 'uv run -m baseline.mcp_copilot.arg_generation') before evaluation. It is not induced online from the agent's own trajectories.
index_structure_topology: Hierarchical server -> tool topology over a dense vector index. The MCP server-tool architecture is explicitly exploited: each server exposes multiple related tools with contextual descriptions. Retrieval uses both a server-level description embedding and a tool-level description embedding (cosine similarities s_server and s_tool combined per the MCP-Zero score). The repo exposes TOP_SERVERS and TOP_TOOLS knobs, confirming a two-level (server-then-tool) hierarchical retrieval index rather than a flat tool list.
retriever_type: dense (embedding-similarity) retriever, off-the-shelf. Server-level summaries are generated by Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct and embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B; queries are embedded the same way; candidates are ranked by cosine similarity using the MCP-Zero hierarchical score. No learned/contrastively-trained retriever; BM25/sparse not used. An embedding-model ablation swaps Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B for BGE-M3 (minor drop 78.95%->76.84%, p=0.84).
retriever_learning_signal: none (off-the-shelf): the retriever is a frozen dense embedding model (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, alternatively BGE-M3) with a fixed hierarchical cosine-similarity scoring rule borrowed from MCP-Zero. It is not trained with contrastive similarity labels, LM-feedback, downstream-task-effectiveness/preference, RL, or value-based signals. The paper's analysis explicitly attributes the bottleneck to 'the current tool-retrieval methodology itself rather than a specific embedding model or hyperparameter', motivating (but not implementing) learned retrieval.
query_construction: LLM-generated structured query produced by the agent at Route time: the prompt requires the query to contain a <tool_assistant> tag with a server-intent field and a tool-intent field, e.g. '<tool_assistant>server: <platform/permission domain> tool: <operation type + target></tool_assistant>'. The agent (the benchmarked LLM) thus constructs an intent-decomposed query specifying the desired server domain and tool operation, rather than passing the raw user task verbatim. Query errors (13.33% of failures) arise from semantic-irrelevance or granularity-mismatch in this generated query.
query_granularity: step/sub-task level (with a two-level server+tool structure): each Route call issues a query for the tool(s) needed at the current step of the rollout; the agent re-queries as the plan unfolds and after errors. The query itself is internally two-level (server-intent and tool-intent fields), matching the hierarchical index. Not a single task-level one-shot retrieval at t=0.
when_to_retrieve: iterative / agent-initiated within a ReAct loop: there is no fixed retrieve-then-execute pipeline ('always retrieving before executing may fail when outputs must be combined or when re-routing is required after errors'). The agent decides when to emit a Route action versus an Execute or Response action, retrieving repeatedly across the multi-step trajectory as needed (average 1.19-4.35 Route calls per task depending on model).
retrieval_trigger_signal: Agent-initiated request governed by the ReAct policy / prompt heuristics: the route-tool prompt instructs the LLM to call Route when it cannot solve the task with currently available tools, when a new/unknown task arises, or when the request is vague/complex and feasible tools must first be explored (the 'discovery' phase). There is no learned router, token-confidence, or uncertainty estimator; the trigger is the LLM emitting a Route action under these prompt guidelines, plus re-routing after Execute failures.
reranking: No explicit second-stage reranker. Candidate tools are scored once by the MCP-Zero hierarchical formula score=(s_server x s_tool) x max(s_server, s_tool), which fuses server-level and tool-level cosine similarities (a hierarchy-aware scoring rule rather than a cross-encoder rerank), and the top-k=5 are returned directly. No cross-encoder, RRF, or instruction-tuned reranking stage.
retrieved_context_refinement: Minimal: retrieved tool descriptions (top-k) are passed to the agent largely as-is for it to choose and parameterize an Execute call. A server-summary step (Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct generates concise server-level summaries used as the server-level embedding key) is an index-side, pre-retrieval engineering step rather than post-retrieval refinement. There is no decompose-recompose, reason-in-documents distillation, distractor filtering, or compression applied to retrieved candidates at inference.
how_retrieved_used: prompt augmentation within an agentic loop: the top-k retrieved tool descriptions (from Route) are injected into the agent's context so it can reason about and select which tool to Execute and with what parameters; the tool's execution output is fed back as an observation. There is no fine-tuning/training signal and no latent-token injection; benchmarked models are used zero-shot.
planning_integration: retrieve-then-act interleaved inside a ReAct loop over a POMDP. The MCP Copilot Agent unifies reasoning and acting with three actions (Route=retrieve k tools, Execute=invoke a tool, Response=finish). Planning is implicit/dynamic: rather than a fixed plan-then-retrieve pipeline, the agent adaptively alternates Route and Execute, re-routing after errors and composing outputs across tools (per-step interleaved retrieval). No MCTS/tree search; planning emerges from the LLM's ReAct reasoning conditioned on retrieved tool descriptions and execution feedback.
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: per-tool-call / per-step within a rollout: each Route is interleaved with the agent's reasoning at the step where a (new) tool is needed, and Execute calls are interleaved between retrievals; retrieval and tool execution are woven into the ReAct reasoning at the granularity of individual agent steps (average ~8-26 dialogue turns per task across models).
adaptation_mechanism: N/A (not framed as CBR): the closest analogue is that the agent reads a retrieved tool's description/schema and instantiates a correctly-parameterized Execute call from it (parameter slot-filling grounded in the retrieved doc); Tool Errors (18.33%) capture failures of this grounding (e.g., passing 'path name' instead of 'path'). No adaptation of prior solved cases.
retrieved_item_representation: Structured tool documentation injected as text: each retrieved candidate is the tool's name, server context, parameter schema, and natural-language description (server-level summaries generated by Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct feed the server embedding). It is raw tool documentation, not a distilled strategy, free-text workflow, executable program/skill, or latent token.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Raw documentation / single reference item: the retrieved unit is a concrete MCP tool specification (name + parameter schema + description) within its server context, not a distilled strategy, state-aware guideline, reusable workflow, or procedural skill.
noise_robustness_mechanism: Limited / largely absent in the baseline; the benchmark exposes the lack of robustness as a finding. The agent can re-route and retry Execute (up to 3 repetitions per the prompt) when calls fail, providing rudimentary error recovery, but there is no relevance evaluator, self-reflection module, distractor-aware training, or reason-in-documents refinement. The error analysis shows Retrieve Errors (50%) and Other Errors (18.33%, e.g., abandoning a task on a network timeout without retry) dominate, and the authors explicitly call for future systems with better retrieval robustness, failure recovery, and adaptive tool exploration.
memory_type: none: the MCP Copilot Agent has no episodic/skill/workflow/graph/latent memory store. The toolset is a static external library, not an agent-written memory; multi-step dialogue context is kept in-context but not a retrievable learned memory. The error analysis notes a 'need for more sophisticated memory mechanisms' as future work, implying current memory is absent.
write_back: false: the agent does not write new experiences, cases, or skills back into any retrievable memory during evaluation. Task/tool/key-point data are created offline (human annotation), not via test-time write-back.
online_growth: false within an evaluation run: the LiveMCPTool index is fixed (frozen Docker toolset) and does not grow from the agent's outputs at test time. (Separately, the LiveMCPEval framework is designed to allow the BENCHMARK to be expanded with new servers/tasks over time without manual annotation, but that is benchmark maintenance, not agent test-time memory growth.)
write_back_trigger: never: no automatic memory write-back exists. Tasks and verified key points are produced by a two-stage human proposer/validator pipeline offline; the agent does not persist successes or failures to memory at inference time.
failure_experience_usage: N/A / none for the agent: failed experiences are not stored or retrieved as negative cases. The PAPER does conduct a rich post-hoc human error analysis of agent failure trajectories (Query Error 13.33%, Retrieve Error 50.00%, Tool Error 18.33%, Other Error 18.33% on Claude-family trajectories), but these are diagnostic categories, not a failure-memory the agent learns from.
memory_evolution_update: N/A: there is no agent-written memory to mutate. The static LiveMCPTool is updated only by maintainers (e.g., removing broken tools, version fixes in the repo), not via append/dedup/refine of agent memory.
retrieval_as_learned_policy: No: tool retrieval uses a fixed dense-embedding hierarchical top-k scoring rule (MCP-Zero formula) with frozen embeddings; it is not an RL- or value-learned retrieval policy. The agent's decision of WHEN/WHAT to Route is made by the prompted LLM (ReAct), but the ranking function itself is fixed cosine-similarity scoring, and the agent is run zero-shot without policy training.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: No: single-agent evaluation; each benchmarked LLM operates its own MCP Copilot Agent over a private (per-run) toolset with no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing. (Multiple human annotators collaborate to BUILD the benchmark, but that is dataset construction, not shared retrievable agent memory.)
benchmarks: LiveMCPBench (introduced by this paper): 95 multi-step real-world daily tasks across 6 domains (Office, Lifestyle, Leisure, Finance, Travel, Shopping); LiveMCPTool = 70 MCP servers with 527 tools (taxonomized into ~8 server/tool classes incl. Discovery, Visualization, File Access, Code, Entertainment, Finance, Location, Miscellaneous), packaged in Docker, all retrieving genuine real-time data (no simulation). Annotators used 55/70 servers (78.57%) and 150/527 tools (28.46%). LiveMCPEval = an LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation framework (DeepSeek-V3-0324 default judge) achieving ~81% agreement with human reviewers. Table 1 compares against API-Bank, ToolBench, tau-bench, MCPBench, MCP-RADAR, MCP-Zero (toolset only), MCPEval.
benchmark_family: tool (tool/MCP-use benchmark). Specifically an MCP-agent benchmark in the lineage of tool-use benchmarks (API-Bank, ToolBench/ToolLLM, tau-bench) and MCP benchmarks (MCPBench, MCP-RADAR, MCPEval); it is the first to stress LARGE-SCALE retrieval + multi-tool composition over a real, plug-and-play MCP toolset of dozens of servers.
baselines: Models benchmarked as agents (the 'baselines' are the 12 frontier LLMs driving the single MCP Copilot Agent): Claude-Sonnet-4-20250514, Claude-Opus-4-20250514, GPT-5, GPT-5-Mini, GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1-Mini, Gemini-2.5-Pro, DeepSeek-V3-0324, DeepSeek-R1-0528, Qwen3-235B-A22B, Qwen3-32B, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct (leaderboard adds GLM-4.5, Kimi-K2). The MCP Copilot Agent (ReAct + MCP-Zero hierarchical retrieval) is itself the baseline agent scaffold. Retrieval-config baselines/ablations: k in {1,5,10}; embedding models Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B vs BGE-M3. Evaluator baselines: DeepSeek-V3 vs Qwen2.5-72B vs others as LLM judges, plus majority-vote and human annotation. Prior benchmarks contrasted in Table 1 (API-Bank, ToolBench, tau-bench, MCPBench, MCP-RADAR, MCP-Zero, MCPEval) are positioning baselines, not run head-to-head.
key_metrics: Primary: task success rate (single-run) under LiveMCPEval's binary LLM-as-a-Judge classification J=Evaluator(Task, KeyPoints, Trajectory, ToolDescriptions) in {Success, Failure}. Efficiency metrics (Table 2): average dialogue Steps, average used Tools, average Execute calls, average Route (retrieval) calls, total Tokens consumed (millions), and monetary cost (for the Pareto frontier). Evaluator-reliability metrics: human-agreement rate, F1 vs human, Kendall's tau-b rank correlation between evaluators. Suggested alternatives: pass@k, pass^k. No standalone Recall@k/nDCG retrieval metrics are reported.
headline_result: Claude-Sonnet-4 reaches the highest task success rate of 78.95% on LiveMCPBench (DeepSeek-V3 judge), while most other frontier models score only 30-50% (e.g., Claude-Opus-4 70.53%, GPT-5 52.63%, Qwen3-235B-A22B 48.42%, down to Qwen3-32B 30.53%). Retrieval errors account for ~50% of all failures (the single largest error category), establishing tool retrieval as the dominant bottleneck; active tool composition correlates with higher success.
ablations: (1) Number of retrieved tools k (Claude-Sonnet-4 agent, DeepSeek-V3 judge): k=5 (main) 78.95%; k=1 drops to 64.21% (exact McNemar p=0.02, significant); k=10 stays at 78.95% (p=1.00, no gain), indicating saturation due to retriever limits, not candidate scarcity. (2) Embedding model: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (78.95%) vs BGE-M3 (76.84%, p=0.84, not significant) -> result robust to embedding choice, bottleneck is the retrieval methodology itself. (3) Evaluator-bias / single-evaluator analysis: re-evaluating all trajectories with Qwen2.5-72B preserves rankings (Kendall tau-b=0.8837, p=0.00008); majority vote over 10 evaluators gives 77.89% human agreement; max (oracle) agreement 97.89%. (4) Evaluator reliability: DeepSeek-V3 78.95-81.05% human agreement, GPT-4.1-Mini/Qwen2.5-72B ~75%, weaker judges (DeepSeek-R1, Claude-Opus-4, Qwen3-32B) 58.95-70% on long trajectories. (5) Key-points source: LLM-generated vs human-annotated key points -> auto-generated key points often match or improve agreement, showing generalizability. (6) Behavioral analysis: active tool composition (more tools/executions) correlates with success (Claude-Sonnet-4: 2.71 tools), but over-exploration shows diminishing returns (Claude-Opus-4: 3.40 tools -> 70.53%); exploration-exploitation balance, not raw tool count, drives performance.
evaluation_decoupling: Partial: intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG) are NOT reported as standalone numbers. Retrieval quality is assessed indirectly via (a) the k and embedding-model ablations on end-to-end success, and (b) a human error-attribution analysis where Retrieve Error = 50% of failures. End-to-end task success rate is the headline metric; retrieval competence is diagnosed through error decomposition rather than decoupled IR metrics.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Both: outcome is the binary task success rate (LLM-as-a-Judge over key points). Process is captured via (i) behavioral/efficiency metrics (steps, tools used, executions, route calls, tokens), (ii) a four-way agent error taxonomy localizing failures to Query / Retrieve / Tool / Other stages of the retrieve-compose pipeline, and (iii) key-point-based evaluation that checks intermediate critical subtasks (each key point auditable from the tool-call log), plus a separate four-way evaluation-error taxonomy for judge reliability.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Explicitly analyzed via a log-price vs performance Pareto frontier (Figure 5). Token consumption (Table 2) ranges from ~1.93M (Qwen3-32B) to 7.16M (Claude-Opus-4); Claude models and GPT-5 consume 6-7M tokens vs 2-3M for others, driven by more aggressive tool exploration and error-recovery trials. Average Route (retrieval) calls per task range 1.19-4.35; Execute calls 1.29-7.24; steps 8.08-25.53. More aggressive tool exploration buys higher success but at substantially higher token cost; the Pareto frontier identifies the most cost-effective models. Monetary cost computed from OpenRouter prices as of Jan 31, 2026 (input+output tokens).
context_budget_and_selection_count: Fixed top-k retrieval: k=5 tools returned per Route call in all main experiments (repo exposes two-level knobs TOP_SERVERS=5, TOP_TOOLS=3). The whole-context injection of 527 tools is explicitly avoided (the motivation for retrieval over a large toolset); only the top-k candidates per Route call enter the prompt, with multiple Route calls across a rollout. The k-ablation (1/5/10) shows k=5 is near-optimal (k=1 budget-starves, k=10 plateaus). No fixed token-budget cap figure; budget is governed implicitly by the per-call top-k and number of agent steps.
benchmark_construction_and_size: Tasks: 95 high-fidelity multi-step daily tasks across 6 domains, distilled from 300 candidate tasks via a two-stage pipeline (two groups of 3 CS-student annotators acting as proposers and validators; LLM-assisted ideation permitted but vetted; each task completed against the real toolset with annotated key points; validators de-duplicate and enforce quality and three principles: real-world relevance, temporal dynamics, tool diversity). Toolset: LiveMCPTool = 70 MCP servers / 527 tools, built by aggregating 5,588 server configs from the mcp.so marketplace, filtering out key-dependent servers, taxonomic curation, expert vetting, and Docker packaging for plug-and-play reproducibility (no scattered API keys); all online tools verified to fetch genuine real-time data. Answer verifiability: medium-high but NOT rule-based ground truth -> LiveMCPEval uses an LLM-as-a-Judge over human/LLM-verified key points to handle dynamic data and multiple valid solution paths (binary success), validated at ~81% human agreement (DeepSeek-V3 judge), F1 87.32 (Claude-Sonnet-4 trajectories) / 83.08 (Claude-Opus-4). Difficulty signal: best system Claude-Sonnet-4 reaches only 78.95% success and most models 30-50%, with retrieval errors ~50% of failures, signaling substantial headroom.
builds_on: MCP-Zero (Fei et al., 2025) for the hierarchical server-tool retrieval scoring formula score=(s_server x s_tool) x max(s_server, s_tool); ReAct (Yao et al., 2023) for the reasoning+acting agent loop; POMDP / Monte-Carlo planning in large POMDPs (Silver & Veness, 2010) for the formal problem framing; LLM-as-a-Judge (Zheng et al., 2023, MT-Bench) for LiveMCPEval; the Model Context Protocol (Anthropic, 2024) as the underlying tool interface; Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct for server summaries and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (alt. BGE-M3) for dense embeddings.
contrasts_with: Prior tool-use benchmarks with simulated/unstable APIs and single-server, in-context tool injection: API-Bank (8 servers/73 tools, rule-based), ToolBench/ToolLLM (unstable, ~55.6% APIs dead), tau-bench (2 servers/28 tools), ToolAlpaca, Seal-Tools, ShortcutsBench, StableToolBench(-MirrorAPI). Prior MCP benchmarks that are small-scale and inject tools directly into context: MCPBench (10 servers, no large-scale retrieval), MCP-RADAR (9 servers/42 tools), MCPEval (12 servers/77 tools, synthetic). Large-scale MCP-retrieval methods it contrasts with on adaptability: RAG-MCP, MCP-Zero, and ScaleMCP (criticized for rigid pipelines lacking adaptive invocation/error recovery; ScaleMCP additionally for a manually-constructed, low-diversity toolset). LiveMCPBench is positioned as the first real + large-scale (70 servers/527 tools) + dynamic + plug-and-play + LLM-judged MCP benchmark requiring genuine large-scale retrieval and multi-tool composition.
lineage: Group E (tool-use). A 2025 large-scale MCP-agent BENCHMARK (with an integral hierarchical dense tool-retrieval component, the Route action / MCP Copilot Agent). It extends the tool-use benchmark lineage (API-Bank -> ToolBench/ToolLLM -> tau-bench) into the MCP era and the MCP-benchmark lineage (MCPBench/MCP-RADAR/MCPEval), and sits alongside large-scale MCP tool-retrieval work (MCP-Zero, RAG-MCP, ScaleMCP). Its central diagnosis is that tool RETRIEVAL over an ocean of MCP tools, plus multi-tool composition, are the unsolved bottlenecks for agentic tool use.
tool_document_engineering: Server-level summary generation as an index-side engineering step: Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct generates concise server-level descriptions (via a dedicated 'server summary' prompt) that, together with tool-level descriptions, are embedded by Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B to form the two-level retrieval keys. Beyond this server-summary augmentation, tool descriptions are used largely as collected (curated/vetted during toolset construction); there is no synthetic-query augmentation, weighted-field embedding, or instruction-tuned tool embedding.
index_content_separation: Yes / progressive disclosure by design: the full 527-tool suite is deliberately NOT injected into context; a lightweight retrievable index (server + tool description embeddings) is separated from the heavy executable tools, and only the top-k retrieved candidates are surfaced on demand via Route, with actual execution deferred to the Execute action. This index-then-content pattern is the core motivation for the benchmark (avoiding prompt bloat / context overflow from thousands of tools).
dynamic_index_and_protocol: Protocol: native Model Context Protocol (MCP) with a server-tool architecture; tools invoked through the agent's Execute action over real MCP servers (local and online). Index: STATIC within an evaluation run (a frozen, Docker-packaged validated toolset of 70 servers/527 tools for reproducibility; broken servers are pruned via repo maintenance, not live auto-sync). The framework is designed to be expandable (new servers/tasks can be added and re-indexed), but there is no automatic CRUD live-synchronization of the index during evaluation (contrast ScaleMCP's auto-synchronizing index, which the paper cites). Real-time DATA is dynamic (genuine live weather/news/stock retrieval), even though the tool INDEX is fixed.
tool_dependency_awareness: Partially, via the hierarchical server-tool scoring rather than explicit dependency modeling. Retrieval is hierarchy-aware (server-level and tool-level similarities are jointly scored, letting server priors dominate when tool matches are weak), and tasks require chaining where one tool's output feeds another (multi-hop, cross-domain composition). However, the retriever does NOT build an inter-tool dependency graph or bipartite KG and does not do dependency-aware reranking; composition/chaining is left to the ReAct agent's reasoning, and Retrieve Errors (50%) include failures to surface tools whose semantic role differs from the query (e.g., 'convert to MP3' vs a tool documented as 'extract audio tracks').
adaptation_mechanism: N/A (not framed as CBR); see retrieved-item usage: the agent grounds Execute-call parameters in the retrieved tool schema (slot-filling) and can retry/re-route on failure (up to 3 Execute retries), but it does not adapt prior solved cases.
